newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BA official says no decision yet on slots.
newsitem.headline: BA official says no decision yet on slots.

text.p: British Airways has not decided yet whether to release slots at London Heathrow airport to win U.K. regulatory approval of its alliance with AMR Corp's American Airlines, a BA official said on Friday.
BA's head of competition and industry affairs Christopher Allen told Reuters that "there was no point in coming to a final position" until all regulatory authorities had completed their assessment.
The deal is currently being vetted by the competition watchdogs in Britain and the United States as well as the European Commission.
But Allen reiterated his company's view that airlines should be able to sell airport landing and taking off slots despite the Commission's view that this is illegal.
"We have not said whether we are prepared even to sell them, but we believe we should be able to sell them (if we want to)," Allen said.
He is in Brussels for a two-day conference on European air transport services and airports.

The U.K.'s Office of Fair Trading said in December it would clear the BA-AA alliance if the companies gave up 168 weekly slots at Heathrow, but European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert says the trading of slots is not acceptable.
AMR's senior vice president Hans Mirka was quoted by the Wall Street Journal Europe on Friday as saying he was prepared to defy the Commission and sell slots at Heathrow.
American has 181 weekly slots at Heathrow, according to BA's Allen.

In reply to a question, he said the slot issue appeared to hold the key to getting antitrust immunity, but he did not think it would be a matter for discussion at talks on an 'open-skies' agreement between Britain and the United States.
"Both governments agree that slots are not a matter for bilateral discussion," he said.
With an open-skies agreement, the congestion at Heathrow would no longer be a problem for other U.S. carriers since they would be given the right to compete with the alliance.
But the accord would not give EU-based airlines the traffic rights they may need, which is another reason why the Commission has expressed competition concerns, participants at the conference said.

Earlier, at the conference, Allen defended the view that slot trading was both "lawful and highly desirable". Current EU rules, which are being revised by the Commission, had done nothing to increase competition at busy airports, he said.
This view was shared by many participants, many of them industry representatives and antitrust lawyers.
"I can't see any reason why slots cannot be sold under the present legal regulation," Trevor Soames, a partner with law firm Norton Rose, told Reuters.
The EU's slot allocation regulation, 95/93/EEC, provides for the exchange of slots, but it does not explicitly prohibit their selling.
The current practice, however, is that slots are paid for either because they do not have the same value or because new entrants simply do not have any.
"Exchanged for what? For money?" said Soames adding that the meaning of that aspect of the regulation was open to interpretation.
But other participants opposed making slot trading unequivocally legal.
Christopher Welsh, secretary general of the European Air Shippers Council, said that slot trading, if made legal, would give "a considerable advantage to incumbent carriers".

This view was shared by Philip Martin, director general of Britain's Air Transport Users Council, who argued that the surrender of slots could not be described as "confiscation" since such rights were not the property of the airlines.

The Commission is expected to make proposals shortly which could allow for the selling of slots. EU transport ministers would have the final word on this, but whatever the new rules may be they will come to late for the BA-AA alliance.
